strengths: Substantial and well-curated dataset of 5,062 human-evaluated proofs with high inter-judge agreement (90.4%, ~5% error rate), providing a valuable resource for the community with commitment to open-sourcing

Rigorous and thoughtful annotation methodology including qualified judges (IMO participants), custom UI, LLM-assisted summaries validated for bias, and systematic quality monitoring (10% double-grading)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation addressing multiple important questions: natural language vs formal reasoning (11x gap), final-answer vs proof-correctness discrepancy (30% for O3), and best-of-n ranking strategies (40% accuracy)
Practical demonstrations of utility including fine-tuned OPC-R1-8B model achieving 88.1% judgment accuracy and reproduction of key empirical findings
Well-organized presentation with extensive reproducible supplementary materials (prompts, grading guidelines, interface screenshots)
weaknesses: Limited novelty in core empirical findings—main claims (final-answer ≠ proof correctness, formal reasoning lags informal, best-of-n helps) are confirmatory of prior suspicions rather than surprising discoveries; limited analysis of why these gaps exist or how to address them

Data contamination concerns inadequately addressed: problems from public competitions likely in training data; no systematic analysis of contamination extent; authors dismiss as 'less critical' despite implications for benchmarking uses

Scope limitations reduce generalization: ~90% high-school level problems, biased toward competitions where LLMs perform reasonably well (~50% accuracy), limited coverage of research-level mathematics, and 'balanced' mix claim overstated (43% correct actual)

Methodological biases in evaluation: MathArena subset only includes solutions with correct final answers (limiting failure analysis), best-of-n evaluation incomplete (full judgments only for 60/152 problems), Putnam comparison altered by appending answers

Limited experimental depth: best-of-n only evaluated on O4-MINI without cross-model experiments, fine-tuned model trains/tests on same distribution, no significance testing or confidence intervals on key claims, missing ablations on design choices

Generalization concerns: all evaluated models are proprietary and very recent (2025), open models significantly underperform, findings may not transfer to future architectures or different problem distributions

Incomplete analysis of concurrent work and limited evidence that OPC improves proof generation (only judging); no statistical tests for differences between models; LLM summary feature introduced mid-annotation could create subtle pattern shifts

strengths: Rigorous dataset construction with careful judge selection (IMO-level), collaborative guideline development, and low estimated noise (5% individual judge error)
Comprehensive validation with ~10% double-grading achieving 90.4% inter-rater agreement, demonstrating high-quality human annotations
Valuable empirical confirmations of important properties (11× informal vs. formal gap, substantial final-answer vs. proof-correctness discrepancy, effectiveness of ranking-based best-of-n)
Demonstrated practical utility by fine-tuning 8B model to match state-of-the-art on proof judgment task
Diverse competition sources with explicit metadata; detailed documentation of methodology, grading interface, and prompts enabling transparency
weaknesses: Limited novelty: dataset construction follows standard practices without novel methodology; findings largely confirmatory rather than surprising, particularly compared to concurrent work (Guo et al. 2025b, Sheng et al. 2025)
Significant scope limitation: ~90% high school-level problems, minimal undergraduate coverage, no research-level mathematics, limiting generalizability beyond competition mathematics

Data contamination inadequately addressed: public competition problems likely in model training data; dismissing this as 'less critical' is problematic for a resource claiming broad downstream utility in training and evaluation

Weak formal vs. informal proof generation comparison: only DeepSeek-Prover-V2 evaluated (not a general-purpose model); different problem distributions (PutnamBench vs. IMO) confound the analysis; needs systematic evaluation of models designed for formal reasoning

Overstated fine-tuning contribution: OPC-R1-8B's 88.1% accuracy explicitly noted as potentially due to train/test overlap with unknown generalization to out-of-distribution data; authors acknowledge performance 'may degrade,' significantly limiting the claimed advance

Scattered incomplete analyses: best-of-n evaluated on only 60 problems with all generations; self-judging results (Table 3) unexplored; no problem characteristic or error analysis; missing computational cost-benefit analysis for expensive O(n²) Swiss ranking

Evaluation design concerns: binary correctness labels lose nuance; only 10% double-graded; LLM issue summaries (E.2) might introduce subtle bias despite agreement checking; high variance in judge backgrounds not addressed

Missing deeper insights: why formal methods underperform (architectural, training, or task design?), what proof properties cause judgment failures, why ranking methods outperform discrete approaches—paper documents phenomena but lacks mechanistic understanding

strengths: Large-scale, high-quality dataset (5,000+ proofs, 1,000+ problems) with rigorous quality assurance (90.4% inter-judge agreement, ~5% estimated error rate)
Exemplary methodology with careful judge selection (IMO participants), detailed grading guidelines, multiple validation procedures, and LLM-assisted bias checks

Comprehensive empirical findings quantifying important gaps: 11x difference between formal and informal proof generation, substantial proof correctness variance despite similar final-answer accuracy, effectiveness of best-of-n strategies
Broad experimental scope evaluating 6 SOTA models, providing useful baselines and insights for mathematical reasoning research
Excellent reproducibility with open-sourced dataset, detailed prompts, grading guidelines, interface documentation, and fine-tuned open-source model
Practical design for downstream usage with appropriate data splits enabling training and evaluation on proof generation tasks
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: binary classification, standard human evaluation pipeline, and LLM summaries are helpful but not novel techniques
Data contamination concern incompletely addressed: public competition problems likely encountered during model training, undermining benchmarking utility despite authors' mitigation arguments
Scope limitations: predominantly high school level problems with minimal undergraduate/advanced mathematics coverage, limiting applicability to broader mathematical reasoning domains

OPC-R1-8B evaluation has significant caveat: train and test sets share identical distribution, with acknowledged risk of substantial OOD performance degradation; no validation on truly held-out benchmarks
Best-of-n findings are incremental: applies known technique to familiar domain with expected results; ranking methods adapted from concurrent work rather than novel contributions

Incomplete mechanistic analysis: limited investigation of why models fail on specific problem types; self-critique failures (Table 3) underexplored; no systematic relationship analysis between final-answer accuracy and proof quality
Findings partially confirmatory: proof accuracy gap and formal proving difficulty align with existing intuitions and concurrent work (Guo et al., 2025b); limited surprising insights
Judge-related limitations: small pool of 13 judges with only 3 experienced in LLM evaluation; no systematic analysis of judge-specific biases or expertise-related patterns

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important bottleneck in mathematical reasoning research through a large-scale, human-evaluated dataset
Exemplary dataset creation methodology with rigorous validation (90.4% inter-judge agreement, 10% double-grading, collaborative guideline development)
Comprehensive experimental analysis addressing three well-motivated open questions with clear practical implications
Large scale (5,062 proofs, 1,010 problems) with diverse problem sources and multiple SOTA models evaluated
Strong reproducibility with complete methodology documentation, prompts, code, and supplementary materials provided
Thoughtful treatment of contamination concerns with empirical evidence showing robustness of conclusions
Practical contribution demonstrated through training OPC-R1-8B model achieving 88.1% judgment accuracy
Clear and well-presented findings with useful guidance (formal vs. informal gap, final-answer vs. proof correctness mismatch, best-of-n effectiveness)
weaknesses: Limited novelty beyond dataset creation; primarily a benchmark paper without novel algorithmic or theoretical contributions
Core findings are somewhat confirmatory rather than surprising (e.g., formal proofs lagging behind natural language proofs)
Scope limited to olympiad-level mathematics (84% high-school, 16% undergraduate); findings may not generalize beyond competition problems
Best-of-n subset relatively small (152 problems, only 60 with all 8 judgments) with large confidence intervals and acknowledged bug affecting 18 questions
OPC-R1-8B evaluation uses train/test split from same distribution (OPC generic), potentially inflating performance; limited external validation
Contamination issue not fully resolved; paper acknowledges it 'cannot be fully ruled out' for main results despite mitigation arguments
Incomplete analysis of inter-judge disagreements (9.6% rate); no systematic investigation of whether disagreements are systematic or which judges are stricter
Limited systematic analysis of failure modes and model behaviors; finding that models rarely acknowledge uncertainty (6.7%) is under-explored
Formal vs. informal comparison fairness concerns; informal models not specifically optimized for this task and formal models underwent significant tuning elsewhere (Seed-Prover)
Statistical rigor concerns in some sections; multiple comparisons without correction and small sample sizes for certain result categories

strengths: Rigorous data collection methodology with careful judge selection, collaborative guideline development, comprehensive quality control (90.4% inter-rater agreement), and extensive documentation
Addresses a genuine gap in the community—the lack of large-scale, human-validated proof datasets from high-quality competitions
Provides concrete empirical answers to three previously open questions about proof generation capabilities
Strong reproducibility commitment with dataset, code, and detailed methodology in supplementary materials
Thoughtful engagement with data contamination concerns through multiple validation approaches
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the paper is primarily a benchmark/dataset contribution applying standard annotation practices rather than introducing novel technical methods or insights

Unresolved data contamination concerns undermine key findings: authors acknowledge they cannot conclusively attribute the GEMINI-2.5-PRO vs O4-MINI performance gap to genuine differences rather than contamination

Severely restricted scope limits broader impact: ~84% high-school level problems, no research-level mathematics or non-olympiad domains; only 5,000 proofs across 1,000 problems provides limited per-problem coverage

Findings are confirmatory rather than surprising: gaps between formal/informal reasoning, answer accuracy vs. proof correctness, and best-of-n benefits are largely expected behaviors rather than novel discoveries

Significant experimental limitations: best-of-n evaluation uses only 60 problems with full judgments; known bug in Rank (Swiss) method affecting 18 excluded questions; OPC-R1-8B test set shares training distribution, inflating results; performance degrades substantially on out-of-distribution data
Overclaimed results: title 'LLMs Are Human Level Judges' misleading for 89.3% vs 90.4% gap; comparison of different model types conflates confounding factors; practical implications unclear

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: limited explanation of why best-of-n methods work, superficial error pattern analysis in Appendix E, insufficient investigation of performance variance across models
Human baseline comparison issues: baseline measured on different data than test set, affecting judge performance comparisons and validity of claims about model capabilities

strengths: Addresses a critical gap: First large-scale, human-validated dataset of LLM-generated proofs, filling a clear need in the field
Exceptionally rigorous methodology: Expert judges (IMO participants), careful pilot phase with 35% double-grading, high inter-rater agreement (90.4%), and thoughtful interface design
Substantial scale and scope: 5,062 proofs across 1,010 problems from multiple prestigious competitions, covering 6 state-of-the-art models
Addresses important open questions: Resolves debates on formal vs. informal proofs (4× gap), final-answer accuracy gaps (O3 drops 30%), and best-of-n effectiveness (improves to 47%)
Demonstrates practical utility: Fine-tuned OPC-R1-8B achieves 88.1% accuracy, matching frontier models and approaching human-level performance (90.4%)
Excellent reproducibility: Complete dataset release, all prompts documented, detailed methodology, code with instructions, grading interface provided
Thoughtful treatment of limitations: Contamination analysis, out-of-distribution evaluation, uncertainty mechanisms, and comprehensive validation procedures
Rich qualitative analysis: Documents common failure modes (inequality handling, synthetic geometry reasoning, overgeneralization) with concrete examples
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Primarily a dataset contribution; evaluation approach is straightforward binary correctness judgments; fine-tuning uses standard GRPO without novel techniques
Scope constraints: 84% high-school competition problems; limited coverage of advanced/research-level mathematics; mostly closed-form problems not representative of open mathematical research
Model coverage timing issues: GROK-4 and GPT-5 only included as judges, not provers; dataset constructed before their release; inconsistent model coverage across problems

Contamination cannot be fully ruled out: While competition-based analysis suggests difficulty dominates, authors acknowledge GEMINI-2.5-PRO vs O4-MINI gap 'cannot be conclusively attributed to genuine performance differences'
Best-of-n evaluation limitations: Only 152 problems in subset (60 with all 8 generations), large confidence intervals, single-model evaluation (O4-MINI), bug in Rank (Swiss) excluded 18 samples
OPC-R1-8B performance caveats: Training and test sets share distribution (both high-school level); main result (88.1%) may somewhat overestimate generalization despite reasonable OOD performance
Incomplete human baseline: Derived from ~10% double-graded subset rather than test set; potential systematic differences between human and LLM judges not thoroughly explored
Analysis depth: Limited investigation of which mathematical skills are hardest; brief treatment of problem-category effects (§C.2); formal proof comparison limited to single model
